lessons.title: Create a character
lessons.tip: A fiction character feels real when we know what they want, what stops them, and one small detail only they have. Give them a want (to win a race), a flaw (too proud to ask for help) and a habit or an object (always twists a ring). Then show them making a choice.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

lessons.title: Setting and mood
lessons.tip: Setting is where and when a scene happens. It also sets the mood: a quiet lake feels calm, a crowded station feels tense. Choose two or three details that create the feeling you want, instead of describing everything.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

options: The station was packed, and every clock ticked louder than the last.
The lake was calm and still.
The room was quiet and warm.
accepted: The station was packed, and every clock ticked louder than the last.

lessons.title: Use the five senses
lessons.tip: Good description uses all five senses, not only sight: what we see, hear, smell, taste and touch. One precise detail can make a scene alive. “The bread smelled of warm butter” tells more than “The bread was nice.”
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

lessons.title: Show, don’t tell
lessons.tip: Telling states a feeling: “He was nervous.” Showing lets the reader see it: “His hands shook as he checked the clock again.” Show the important moments through actions, words and the body. Use telling for small, quick facts.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

lessons.title: Write dialogue
lessons.tip: Dialogue should sound like real people: short lines, interruptions, and a different voice for each speaker. Use “said” for most lines, and start a new paragraph for each new speaker. Good dialogue also shows what people want or hide.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

activities.prompt: Which tag is the plainest and best for most lines?

options: “Good morning, my esteemed colleague, how fare you?”
“Salutations. I observe that you are early.”

activities.answer: Real people speak in short bursts

accepted: “I’m fine,” she said, and quickly closed the door.

lessons.title: Point of view
lessons.tip: Point of view (POV) is who tells the story. First person uses “I”: we know only what the narrator knows. Third person limited uses “he” or “she” but stays close to one character’s thoughts. Omniscient sees into everyone’s mind. Pick one and stay with it in a scene.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

activities.prompt: Which sentence is first person?
activities.answer: I opened the door and froze.

options: I opened the door and froze.
She opened the door and froze.
They opened the door and froze.
accepted: I opened the door and froze.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is third person?
activities.answer: He opened the door and froze.

options: He opened the door and froze.
I opened the door and froze.
You open the door and freeze.
accepted: He opened the door and froze.

activities.prompt: In first person, what does the reader know?
Which sentence goes inside two characters’ minds (omniscient)?

options: Ana feared the test, while Ben secretly hoped she would fail.
accepted: Ana feared the test, while Ben secretly hoped she would fail.

activities.prompt: Which sentence stays close to one character (third limited)?
activities.answer: Ana’s stomach twisted as she looked at the first question.

options: Ana’s stomach twisted as she looked at the first question.

accepted: Ana’s stomach twisted as she looked at the first question.

activities.prompt: Why keep a consistent point of view in a scene?

activities.answer: Choose who tells the story | Decide how much they know | Keep that view through the scene

items: Keep that view through the scene

lessons.title: Plot shape
lessons.tip: A simple plot has a beginning (meet the character and the problem), a rising middle (things get harder), a climax (the biggest moment) and an ending (what changes). Each step should follow from the one before: because of this, then that.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)

activities.prompt: What happens in the climax?
What belongs in the beginning?
What does the rising middle do?
activities.answer: Makes things harder for the character

options: Makes things harder for the character
accepted: Makes things harder for the character

activities.prompt: Which links events best?

options: And then, and then, and then

activities.prompt: Put the plot parts in order.
Put the story events in order.
activities.answer: Mina signs up for the race but feels slow. | She trains alone and falls behind. | On race day she nearly quits at the hill. | She keeps going and finishes, proud of her own pace.

She trains alone and falls behind.
On race day she nearly quits at the hill.
She keeps going and finishes, proud of her own pace.

lessons.title: Beginnings and endings
lessons.tip: Begin as close to the action as you can: a moment, a question, a problem. Skip long background. End with a change, not a summary: show what is different for the character now. A good ending feels both surprising and right.
sources: Freytag, Technique of the Drama (public domain): the shape of a plot (concept only)
Aristotle, Poetics (public domain translations), and common creative-writing craft teaching (concepts only; all examples original)
